strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful computer-vision problem: connecting observed human surface deformation to an explicit internal anatomical representation. Combining real surface measurements with a layered, pose-driven model is a promising direction for digital-human animation.

SKIM represents a substantial acquisition effort, with five subjects, 45 minutes of multiview recordings, tracked marker trajectories, skeletal poses, and fitted anatomical templates. These paired observations could support useful research on subject-specific soft-tissue deformation.

The formulation clearly separates muscle displacement from skin residual displacement and combines surface supervision with geometric regularization. Propagating the learned deformation to individual muscle meshes provides a practical animation output.

Table 2 demonstrates improvements over scan-based LBS in median surface error (15.64 to 11.51 mm), P90 error (26.03 to 19.20 mm), and the highest-threshold dynamic-region error (134.28 to 64.52 mm). These improvements are valuable even though mean surface error does not improve.

The ablations provide evidence that regularization improves volume stability, particularly for the outer tissue layer. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges dependence on fitted anatomy, the marker suit, and subject-specific training.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering internal muscle deformation is not adequately validated. Internal anatomy comes from an existing surface-to-anatomy fitting method, while measured supervision covers only suit-surface markers. Equation 6 leaves muscle and skin residuals ambiguous, and the reported internal metrics largely measure satisfaction of the imposed priors. Neither the qualitative images nor these metrics establish that inferred individual-muscle shapes match actual anatomy. Targeted internal measurements or a controlled experiment with known internal deformation would materially strengthen the scientific case.

The physical guarantees are overstated. Section 5.2 claims strict avoidance of interpenetration and guaranteed physical plausibility, but Table 2 reports nonzero intersection rates of 0.85% and 0.93%, identical to LBS, and 10.35% muscle-volume deviation. A finite signed-prism-volume penalty does not guarantee collision freedom; positive aggregate prism volume also does not rule out local inversion or nonlocal intersection. Moreover, outer-layer volume is evaluated in canonical space, so its 1.37% error does not establish incompressibility after posing.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of the anatomical decomposition. HIT has a very large surface error (115.34 mm), which the paper itself attributes to template mismatch, making it a weak control for the proposed dynamic formulation. A subject-specific surface-only corrective model trained on the same markers, followed by the same anatomical transfer, would help determine whether the coupled model adds value beyond personalized surface fitting. The architecture ablations retain the proposed formulation and do not answer this question.

The model conditions only on instantaneous skeletal pose, despite claims about spatio-temporal muscle behavior and active bulging. Identical poses can have different muscle shapes under different loads, co-contraction, or motion histories. The formulation cannot distinguish these cases, and no experiment characterizes this limitation. The evidence supports pose-dependent anatomical animation more strongly than general recovery of muscle dynamics.

Experimental and implementation details are insufficient in the supplied manuscript. It does not specify sequence-level train/test assignments, motion coverage, per-subject results, marker counts and coverage, network construction, training settings, or numerical regularization weights. Important metric definitions and the individual-muscle binding procedure are deferred to supplementary material that is not included in the supplied PDF. Consequently, unseen-motion generalization and reproducibility are difficult to assess.

The fidelity and practical scope of the acquisition pipeline need stronger evidence. Tracking fabric does not necessarily measure skin motion because of suit sliding, stretching, and compression, and skeletal estimates are treated as ground truth without an accuracy analysis. These errors can enter the residuals labeled as soft-tissue deformation. The scalability and cost-effectiveness claims also lack acquisition-cost or runtime measurements, despite requiring a 120-camera capture studio and a separate 140-camera scanner.

strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile computer vision problem: connecting observable surface deformation to explicit internal anatomy. The integration of dense surface tracking, layered anatomical templates, pose-dependent deformation, and individual-muscle animation is potentially useful for personalized digital humans.

SKIM represents a substantial acquisition effort, reporting five subjects and 45 minutes of multi-view recordings with tracked marker correspondences, poses, and fitted anatomical templates. These surface observations could support further research even without measured internal anatomy.

The experiments demonstrate useful surface-deformation improvements. In Table 2, SOMA reduces median marker error from 15.64 to 11.51 mm and P90 from 26.03 to 19.20 mm relative to LBS; DRE above the 25 mm threshold decreases from 134.28 to 64.52 mm. Table 4 also shows that regularization improves the reported volume-preservation metrics. The paper acknowledges subject specificity and dependence on anatomical initialization.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering anatomically accurate muscle deformation is not adequately validated. Internal anatomy is fitted from the outer scan using an existing method, while the measured supervision consists of suit-marker displacements. Equation 8 observes only Dskin = Dmusc + Dres: changes to one component can be canceled by the other without changing the data loss. Geometric regularizers select a decomposition but do not establish that it matches actual muscle behavior. Surface error and volume/intersection metrics therefore support plausible animation more strongly than anatomical recovery. Some independent internal validation, even restricted to a body region or controlled experiment, is needed to substantiate the stronger claims.

The pose-only formulation limits the claimed recovery of spatio-temporal muscle behavior and active bulging. Both networks receive the current skeletal pose, without activation, external load, motion history, or current surface residuals. Consequently, the model cannot distinguish different contractions or loading conditions at the same pose. The introduction recognizes these factors, but the evaluation does not test this ambiguity or clearly delimit the method to pose-conditioned deformation.

Claims of guaranteed physical plausibility and strict avoidance of interpenetration in Section 5.2 exceed both the formulation and the results. A finite signed-volume penalty is not a collision guarantee, and positive prism volumes do not exclude all intersections. Table 2 reports nonzero intersection ratios of 0.85% and 0.93%, identical to LBS, with 10.35% deep-tissue volume deviation. Moreover, the subcutaneous volume constraint is evaluated in canonical space, so its low error does not establish incompressibility after posing.

The comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the value of the anatomical decomposition. HIT has a substantial template/proportion mismatch, acknowledged by the authors, and its 115.34 mm mean marker error makes it a weak control for personalized dynamic reconstruction. SOMA's global mean error is slightly worse than LBS, although its median and tail errors improve. A surface-only pose-corrective model trained on the same data, and a simpler deformation-transfer alternative, would clarify whether the proposed coupling adds value beyond fitting personalized surface corrections. The architecture ablations do not answer this question.

Experimental reporting in the supplied manuscript is insufficient to assess generalization and reproducibility. It does not specify the sequence split, motion coverage, per-subject results, marker counts and coverage, network configuration, training schedule, or numerical regularization weights. Essential metric definitions and individual-muscle binding details are deferred to supplementary material that is not included in the supplied PDF. The stated availability of data and code has no identifiable access link in the manuscript, and the interactive/scalability claims lack runtime and resource measurements.

The fidelity of the measured supervision needs characterization. Markers track a stretchable suit rather than skin directly, and pose estimates come from a markerless capture system; suit slip, fabric deformation, pose error, and rigging mismatch can therefore enter the residuals labeled as soft-tissue deformation. No independent error analysis quantifies these effects. This matters because the inferred muscle deformations are justified through those residuals. The 120-camera capture system and separate 140-camera scanner also require a more qualified discussion of acquisition accessibility and cost.

strengths: The paper addresses a worthwhile computer-vision problem: connecting observable human surface motion to explicit internal anatomy. Integrating surface capture, layered deformation learning, and individual-muscle animation is a promising contribution beyond conventional surface-only body models.

SKIM provides potentially useful infrastructure: five subjects, 45 minutes of multi-view recordings, tracked marker correspondences, skeletal poses, and fitted anatomical templates. The canonical correspondence and residual-estimation pipeline is clearly motivated.

The coupled muscle-plus-skin formulation is coherent as an animation model. Separate corrective fields and geometric regularization provide a practical way to balance observed surface motion with internal structural constraints.

The experiments show meaningful benefits over scan-based LBS in selected metrics: median marker error decreases from 15.64 to 11.51 mm, P90 from 26.03 to 19.20 mm, and high-deformation-region error from 134.28 to 64.52 mm. The ablations also demonstrate substantially improved volume preservation with the complete regularization.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering subject-specific muscle deformation is insufficiently validated. Internal anatomy is fitted from the exterior using an existing method, and individual muscles inherit deformations from an aggregate boundary. Supervision measures only the sum of muscle and skin displacements, leaving their decomposition ambiguous. Surface accuracy and agreement with the same geometric priors used during training establish plausibility, but do not establish internal anatomical accuracy. Independent evidence, even for a limited region or controlled setting, is needed to substantiate the main claim.

The model takes instantaneous skeletal pose as input, without activation, external load, or motion history. It therefore cannot distinguish different contractions or dynamic tissue states at the same pose. Claims about recovering spatio-temporal muscle behavior and active bulging exceed what this formulation demonstrates; the supported interpretation is person-specific pose-conditioned anatomical animation.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed anatomical contribution. HIT uses a different representation and generic template, and its 115.34 mm mean surface error suggests substantial fitting or correspondence differences. A person-specific surface-only corrective model trained on identical observations, together with a simpler anatomical deformation-transfer baseline, would better establish the benefit of the coupled formulation. Global mean tracking error is slightly worse than LBS, and architecture ablations produce nearly identical high-deformation-region errors.

Claims of guaranteed physical plausibility and strict avoidance of interpenetration are unsupported. Signed prism-volume penalties are soft local constraints, not general collision guarantees. Table 2 still reports 0.85% and 0.93% intersections, identical to LBS, and 10.35% deep-tissue volume deviation. Moreover, subcutaneous volume is evaluated in canonical space, so that result does not establish its preservation after articulation. These limitations materially qualify the physical claims.

Experimental reporting is too incomplete to assess generalization and reproducibility confidently. The supplied manuscript does not specify sequence splits, per-subject results, motion coverage, detailed DRE aggregation, network construction, training settings, or numerical loss weights. Several essential details are deferred to supplementary material that is not included here. Runtime and hardware measurements are also absent despite real-time and scalability claims.

The accuracy of the supervision itself is not established. Markers track a stretchable suit, while skeletal poses come from a markerless capture system; suit slippage, tracking noise, and pose or rigging errors can all enter the residuals attributed to soft-tissue deformation. Quantifying these effects is particularly important for interpreting the dataset as evidence of muscle behavior. Overall, the promising pipeline and surface-level gains do not yet resolve the evidential gap around internal recovery.

strengths: The paper addresses an interesting computer-vision problem: learning internal anatomical deformation from external observations. The combination of subject-specific anatomy, surface supervision, and coupled muscle/skin deformation is a potentially useful contribution to digital-human modeling.

SKIM represents substantial acquisition effort: five subjects, approximately 225 minutes of recordings, dense marker trajectories, skeletal poses, and fitted anatomical templates. The supplementary material documents acquisition, preprocessing, network architecture, and training parameters.

Table 2 demonstrates meaningful improvements over LBS in median surface error (15.64 to 11.51 mm), P90 error (26.03 to 19.20 mm), and highly dynamic regions (134.28 to 64.52 mm at the highest threshold). Muscle-layer volume deviation also decreases from 18.81% to 10.35%.

The architecture and regularization ablations help characterize the formulation. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges template errors, subject specificity, marker-suit requirements, and unmodeled force-dependent variation.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering internal muscle deformation remains insufficiently validated. Supervision observes only the sum of muscle displacement and skin residual, while anatomy is initialized through template fitting rather than measured internally. Volume and intersection metrics primarily assess the imposed priors; they do not establish that the inferred muscle/skin decomposition matches actual anatomy. Full-body dynamic MRI is not necessary, but some independent regional validation or controlled recovery experiment is needed to distinguish anatomical recovery from plausible animation.

The generalization protocol is underspecified. Section 5 refers to unseen poses and motion sequences, but neither the main text nor supplement specifies the training/validation allocation, held-out exercises, temporal separation, or subject-wise aggregation. Per-subject and per-motion results, dynamic-region sample counts, and variability are absent. Consequently, the strength and consistency of the reported generalization cannot be assessed.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution. HIT uses a different surface representation and obtains 115.34 mm mean error, versus approximately 13 mm for scan-based methods; the paper itself attributes much of this gap to anatomical misalignment. A matched, person-specific surface-corrective model and a simpler deformation-transfer baseline would better establish the benefit of explicitly separating muscle and skin. The architecture ablations retain the proposed formulation and do not answer this question. Overall mean tracking error also slightly worsens relative to LBS.

Claims of guaranteed physical plausibility and strictly avoiding interpenetration are stronger than the formulation or results support. A finite penalty on integrated signed prism volume does not guarantee positive local Jacobians or prevent arbitrary collisions. Table 2 still reports 0.85% and 0.93% intersections, identical to LBS, and 10.35% muscle-volume deviation. Furthermore, nearest-triangle displacement transfer to individual muscles does not establish preservation of each muscle's volume or mutual nonintersection.

The interpretation of the captured residuals as muscle behavior lacks measurement validation. Markers track fabric, and residuals relative to LBS can contain suit motion, pose-estimation error, and skinning-model error in addition to tissue deformation. No quantitative characterization separates these effects. The pose-only predictor also cannot distinguish different loads or contraction states at identical poses, despite those conditions being deliberately included in SKIM; acknowledging this limitation is useful, but the broader dynamic-recovery claims remain insufficiently qualified.

The scalability and cost claims lack supporting measurements. Training acquisition uses 120 cameras, a separate 140-camera scanner, and subject-specific processing, while no inference timing, training cost, or reduced-camera experiment is reported. Cheap pose-driven inference is plausible, but it should be distinguished from the substantial cost of constructing each personalized model.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for computer vision and digital humans: connecting observable surface deformation to explicit internal anatomy. The combination of dense surface capture, layered deformation prediction, and individual-muscle visualization is a useful research direction.

SKIM represents substantial acquisition effort: five subjects, approximately 225 minutes of recordings, dense marker trajectories, and personalized anatomical templates. The supplementary material describes acquisition, tracking refinement, network architecture, and training parameters in useful detail.

The results demonstrate benefits over scan-based LBS on several surface metrics. Table 2 reduces median marker error from 15.64 to 11.51 mm, P90 from 26.03 to 19.20 mm, and DRE above 25 mm from 134.28 to 64.52 mm. Muscle-layer volume deviation also decreases from 18.81% to 10.35%.

The architecture and regularization ablations provide evidence that the proposed components improve geometric regularity, particularly subcutaneous volume preservation. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges template dependence, subject specificity, and unmodeled force and co-contraction effects.
weaknesses: The central claim of recovering internal muscle deformation is insufficiently validated. Equation 8 supervises only the sum of muscle and skin-residual displacements; internal anatomy originates from template fitting rather than subject-specific internal measurements. Surface agreement and volume preservation cannot establish that the inferred muscle deformation is anatomically correct. Full-body dynamic MRI is unnecessary, but some independent validation—such as regional measurements, controlled synthetic recovery, or anatomical expert assessment—is needed to distinguish recovered anatomy from plausible prior-driven animation.

The physical guarantees are overstated. A soft penalty on integrated signed prism volume does not guarantee local non-inversion or prevent all intersections. Table 2 reports nonzero intersection rates of 0.85% and 0.93%, identical to LBS, despite claims of strictly avoiding interpenetration. Moreover, the supplementary transfer mechanism interpolates boundary displacements onto individual muscles without establishing preservation of their volumes or mutual non-intersection. The measured aggregate-layer properties therefore do not justify guarantees for individual anatomy.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. HIT uses a different template and has 115.34 mm mean tracking error, versus 13.11 mm for scan-based LBS; the manuscript itself attributes this largely to anatomical misalignment. This comparison confounds template personalization with deformation modeling. A matched single-layer pose-corrective model followed by the same anatomical transfer, and a prior-driven deformation baseline without learned surface supervision, would clarify whether the proposed decomposition contributes beyond conventional pose-space correction.

Generalization evidence is difficult to assess because the training/validation sequence assignments, split sizes, and motion overlap are not specified. Results lack per-subject and per-motion breakdowns or uncertainty estimates. This matters particularly for repeated exercise sequences and small ablation differences: removing all physical energies changes mean tracking error only from 13.43 to 13.71 mm, while DRE remains nearly unchanged. The current evidence supports geometric regularization more clearly than improved recovery of muscle behavior.

The observation model introduces unquantified confounds. Markers track a fabric suit, and skeletal poses come from a markerless estimation system, yet their residuals are treated as soft-tissue ground truth. Suit slippage, fabric deformation, pose errors, and LBS approximation errors can all contribute to these residuals. The paper provides tracking coverage but no independent assessment separating these effects from actual skin deformation.

The demonstrated scope is narrower than the broad dynamic-recovery and scalability framing. At inference, both networks receive only instantaneous pose, so identical poses necessarily produce identical deformation regardless of load, motion history, or muscle activation. Although this limitation is acknowledged, the dataset's different resistance loads are not used to quantify its consequences. Likewise, claims of real-time, scalable, cost-effective operation lack runtime and resource measurements, while acquisition requires 120 cameras and a separate 140-camera scanner. Assessed as Algorithms/General, the acquisition and animation merits are substantial, but these unresolved validation issues favor weak rejection.

The coupled muscle/skin representation and geometric regularization produce promising improvements. Table 2 reduces median tracking error from 15.64 to 11.51 mm, P90 from 26.03 to 19.20 mm, and deep-tissue volume deviation from 18.81% to 10.35% relative to LBS.

Evaluation does not adequately isolate the proposed method's advantage.
